verdicts.reason: Uses January 17, 2025 as the modernization effective date and filing cutoff, citing pp. 1, 17, and 105.
Applies the final rule to petitions filed on or after January 17, 2025, including initial and extension petitions, citing p. 17.
Distinguishes the final rule from the 2023 NPRM and warns not to treat proposals as operative law.
Identifies beneficiary-centric registration as a separate earlier final rule, not as part of the January 2025 modernization effective date.
States that the separate registration final rule was effective March 4, 2024.
Uses operative regulatory text from pp. 142-146 for fees, maintenance of status, amendments, specialty occupation, and related requirements.
Uses the logical-connection standard between the required degree and job duties from p. 145.
Allows a range of qualifying degree fields when each is directly related to the duties, citing p. 145.
States that a general degree without further specialization is insufficient where it alone qualifies for the position.
Explains that 'normally' does not mean 'always' under the specialty-occupation criteria, citing p. 145.
Separates the specialty-occupation definition from the requirement to satisfy at least one listed criterion.
Includes the parallel-positions-in-similar-U.S.-industry route as a regulatory criterion.
Includes the employer or qualifying third-party normal degree requirement route.
Includes the specialized, complex, or unique duties route and associated specialized knowledge.
Recognizes deference to a prior eligibility determination involving the same parties and facts, citing p. 143.
Lists material error, material change, and new material adverse information as exceptions to deference.
Requires evidence of maintained status for extension/amendment requests and identifies paystubs, W-2s, wage reports, tax returns, contracts, and work orders.
Distinguishes DOL LCA certification from USCIS specialty-occupation adjudication, citing p. 144.
Requires filing the amended or new petition before the material change and notes the approval/portability rules for changed work.
Treats a geographic move requiring a corresponding certified LCA as a material change requiring a new or amended petition.
Recognizes the same-area-of-intended-employment exception absent other material changes.
The answer does not mention the itinerary requirement or its removal; its general evidence points do not make this specific point.
Uses more than 50% ownership or majority voting rights as the controlling-interest test.
Allows ownership-related duties only if specialty-occupation duties occupy a majority of the beneficiary's time.
Identifies the up-to-18-month limit for initial approval of a controlling-interest beneficiary's petition.
Identifies the up-to-18-month limit for the first extension and does not assert that all later extensions are invariably capped.
Requires proof at filing of a bona fide position available as of the requested validity start date.
Recognizes that specific day-to-day assignments need not be established for the entire requested period.
Recognizes that USCIS may request contracts, work orders, or similar evidence; it does not treat them as always mandatory.
Uses the third-party organizational-hierarchy staffing test and applies the third party's requirements.
States the cap-gap extension runs to April 1 of the relevant fiscal year or the approved validity start, whichever is earlier.
Preserves the timely-filed, nonfrivolous, cap-subject, change-of-status, and fiscal-year start-date conditions.
Mentions inspections and interviews generally but omits third-party sites, records review, and before/after adjudication detail required by p. 144.
States that inability to verify facts, including failure or refusal to cooperate, may result in denial or revocation.
Translates degree-duty, ownership, and worksite rules into concrete checklist and document-gathering steps.
Keeps employer-specific eligibility and document gaps separate from the January 17 effective date and does not promise approval based on filing date alone.
